stem: Indian citizenship cannot be obtained by –
expl: Under the Citizenship Act, 1955 (as amended from time to time), Indian citizenship can be acquired through the following methods-(1) by birth, (2) by descent, (3) by registration, (4) by naturalization and (5) by incorporation of a territory into India. Depositing money in an Indian bank is a commercial act. It is not a method of acquiring citizenship.

stem: Under which Article of the Constitution of India, Fundamental Rights have been provided to citizens?
expl: In Part III of the Indian Constitution, Fundamental Rights are described in Articles 12 to 35. At present, a total of six Fundamental Rights are provided.

stem: Which one of thé folowing subjects fall within the jurisdiction of both High Court and Supreme Court?

options.label: d
options.text: Protection from the violation of the constitution

expl: Protection/enforcement of Fundamental Rights is a matter that falls within the jurisdiction of both the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226). However, the task of protecting the basic structure of the Constitution also lies within the jurisdiction of both the Supreme Court and the High Courts. The High Courts in India have the power of judicial review and, through writ jurisdiction under Article 226, they can hear cases related to violation of the Constitution and examine the constitutionality of laws and executive orders. The Bihar Public Service Commission has accepted option (c) as the correct answer.

stem: Under which category does the right to constitutional remedies fall?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: The Right to Constitutional Remedies is provided under Part III (Fundamental Rights) of the Constitution, from Article 32 to Article 35. This right is not an independent right in itself; rather, it is the right to enforce other Fundamental Rights. Under this, a person can approach the court in case of violation of Fundamental Rights. Therefore, the Right to Constitutional Remedies falls under-  Fundamental Right  Legal Right  Constitutional Right Hence, option (e) is the correct answer.

stem:
The constitution of India provides for reasonable restrictions on Fundamental Rights but reasonableness must keep in mind that:
1. The interest of the general public is safeguarded
2. Prevailing social válhe and also social needs are not bar
3. Directive principles can be bypassed
4. Collective good is not greater Out of these :
expl: Under Article 19, the freedoms granted (speech, expression, forming associations, free movement, etc.) may be subjected by the State, through law, to reasonable restrictions. From Article 19(2) to Article 19(6), it is provided that such limitations can be imposed only for certain specified purposes—such as the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, protection of the interests of the general public, protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes, and professional/technical schemes, etc.—or in relation to contempt of court, defamation, or incitement to an offence. Therefore, only statements 1 and 2 conform to the constitutional and judicial tests of reasonable restriction, while statements 3 and 4 are both incorrect.

stem: Which of the following writs applies against the illegal detention of a person?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: In the case of a Habeas Corpus petition, the Supreme Court has the power to issue writs under Article 32 of the Constitution. It is an order issued by the court regarding a person who has been kept in custody by another. It is a remedy against forcible/illegal detention. Through it, the detaining authority is directed to produce the detained person before the court within a specified time.

stem: Which of the following rights conferred by the Constitution of India is also available to non-citizens?

options.label: c
options.text: Freedom to Move and Settle in any Part of the Country

expl: The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art. 32) provided by the Indian Constitution is available to non-citizens in relation to those Fundamental Rights which are available to them. It is noteworthy that under Article 300A, the right to property (i.e., a person shall not be deprived of his property except by authority of law) is also available to non-citizens; however, it does not include the right to acquire property [which, in the original Constitution, was available to citizens under Article 19(1)(f)]. In fact, the right to acquire property is no longer a constitutionally guaranteed right.

stem:
Choose the fundamental rights available to Indian Citizen but not to aliens:
I. Freedom of Speech and Expression
II. Equality Before the law
III. Right of Minorities
Iv. Protection of life and liberty

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: The Fundamental Rights in Part III of the Indian Constitution—Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression) and Article 29 (protection of the interests of minority sections)—are available only to Indian citizens; these are not available to non-citizens (foreigners). Whereas Article 14 (equality before law) and Article 21 (protection of life and personal liberty) are available to all persons, i.e., both citizens and foreigners.

stem: When was the Right to Education added through the amendment in the Constitution of India?
expl: Through the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, a new Article 21A was added in Part III of the Constitution, under which the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of 6–14 years. Also, under the amended Directive Principle in Article 45, the State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of 6 years. In the same sequence, the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 was passed by Parliament, which became effective from 1 April, 2010.

expl: Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) the “soul and heart” of the Constitution. Under this right, the writ of certiorari is also called a “post-mortem”.

stem: Which of the following is given the power to enforce the Fundamental Rights by the Constitution?

options.label: d
options.text: The Supreme Court and High Courts

expl: The power to enforce Fundamental Rights is given to the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226). While exercising this power, the courts issue five types of writs—mandamus, habeas corpus, quo warranto, certiorari, and prohibition.

stem: The concept of a welfare state is included in the Constitution of India in-

options.label: a
options.text: The Directive Principles of State Policy

expl: The concept of the Welfare State has been included in the Constitution of India under the Directive Principles of State Policy. These are included in Part IV, under Articles 36 to 51. The Preamble of the Constitution of India also states the objectives of governance, such as ensuring social, economic and political justice; freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; and equality of status and opportunity, which reflect the ideal of a welfare state. Further, the Directive Principles also give directions to the State for establishing a welfare state. Thus, the idea of a welfare state is found in both the Preamble and the Directive Principles. However, if there is no option to select both, then the answer will be the Directive Principles of State Policy.

stem:
Which of the following Directive Principles do not follow Gandhian Principles?
1. Organization of village Panchayats
2. Common Civil Code
3. Promotion of cottage Industry in rural areas
4. Right to work
expl: Statement 1 (Organisation of village panchayats) and 3 (promotion of cottage industries in rural areas) are in accordance with Gandhian principles, whereas statement 2 (Common Civil Code) and 4 (right to work) fall under other categories (liberal–intellectual and socialist) of Directive Principles, not Gandhian. Therefore, the Directive Principles not in accordance with Gandhian principles are 2 and 4.

stem:
Which of the following is/are listed among the Directive Principles in Part-Iv of the Constitution of India?
I. Equal Pay for Equal Work
II. Uniform Civil Code
III. Small family norm
Iv. Education through mother tongue at primary level.

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: In Part IV of the Constitution, Article 39(d) provides for equal pay for equal work for both men and women, and Article 44 lists a Uniform Civil Code for citizens. Article 350A gives a special directive regarding instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage. However, it is not included in Part IV; its effect is similar to a Directive Principle, and it is also not enforceable on the State.

expl: The Directive Principles of State Policy differ from Fundamental Rights because the Directive Principles are non-justiciable, whereas Fundamental Rights are enforceable by courts. Directive Principles are described in Part IV of the Constitution and are directives for establishing a welfare state, whereas Fundamental Rights described in Part III are guarantees of protection given to individuals against the State.

stem: The 10 commandments, which were added by 42nd Amendment Act in Constitution of India, are called as–
expl: In 1976, the Swaran Singh Committee was constituted to give recommendations on constitutional reforms. On the basis of the Swaran Singh Committee’s recommendations, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Part IV-A and, under it, Article 51-A in the Constitution, and 10 Fundamental Duties were included in the Constitution. In 2002, by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, one new Fundamental Duty (related to the education of children in the age group 6–14 years) was added. Therefore, now the number of Fundamental Duties has become 11. The Swaran Singh Committee included 12 members including the Chairman.
